title: Tidewell Telecom - model evaluation, latency/cost, multilingual & tool-calling discovery

Discussed hosted vs dedicated vs private tradeoffs and proposed next steps: run a 2-week benchmark with 3 model variants, share security pack and cost examples, schedule an on-site infra readiness call.

transcript:
Meeting header: 2027-03-11 16:00 UTC | Duration: 63 min | Recording auto
Attendees: Jordan Park (Redwood AE), Maya Singh (Redwood SE), Carlos Mendez (Tidewell CTO), Asha Patel (Head of AI), Liam O'Connor (Infra Lead)

Summary (auto): Discussed model selection for multilingual customer support assistant, need for long context up to 32k tokens for conversation + docs, and tool-calling integration for ticket creation and KB lookup. Reviewed high-level tradeoffs among hosted, dedicated, and private deployment. Agreed next steps and deliverables.

[00:00] Jordan Park: Okay, hey everyone thanks for joining, i'm Jordan from Redwood — i'll kick us off. quick round of intros?
[00:12] Carlos Mendez: Carlos here, CTO at Tidewell. we're trying to move from a rules-based bot to a unified LLM assistant across support and NOC. big constraints are latency during peak hours and strict data residency for EU customers.
[00:28] Asha Patel: Asha — i run the ML team. need models that can handle Spanish and Portuguese natively, and we have long multi-turn conversations plus attached doc contexts, so context length is important.
[00:40] Liam O'Connor: Liam, infra. can we do private? we have some on-prem boxes and also use a cloud VPC with strict peering rules.
[00:48] Jordan Park: great, thanks. Maya from our infra team will cover the technical fit. Maya, i'll hand to you to talk models and deployment options.
[00:55] Maya Singh: hi all. high-level — Redwood supports hosted API for fastest time-to-value, Dedicated reserved pools for predictable throughput, and Private deploy for VPC/on-prem. for model choice: open families like Llama-ish third-gen, Mistrall (sorry mistral) variants, and some quantized Redwood-verified variants we recommend for cost.
[01:18] Carlos Mendez: quick Q — when you say "Redwood-verified" what does that mean in practice? latency numbers? accuracy?
[01:25] Maya Singh: yeah — we run perf benchmarks across context lengths and provide a profile: p50/p95 latency per token, cost per 1k tokens, and quality metrics on our eval sets. for long-context we test up to 32k and report degrade curves.
[01:40] Asha Patel: our main use case is agent desktop where we stitch conversation + ticket history + knowledge articles — often 20-30k tokens in a session. we care about p95 < 1.2s for short queries (few tokens) and overall cost.
[01:55] Jordan Park: that's helpful. two immediate levers — quantization and batching, and also prefix/KV caching for repeated context like KB articles. for p95 under 1.2s we typically point customers to Dedicated for consistent tail latency, but Hosted can sometimes meet it depending on model.
[02:15] Liam O'Connor: what about tool-calling — we need the model to call our ticketing API (create ticket, update status) and also call a retrieval endpoint for KB. is that supported?
[02:24] Maya Singh: yes, tool-calling is supported in our runtime. we have examples for function calls, structured JSON outputs, and a retrieval integration with vector DBs. important: if you go Private and keep the KB on-prem, we can route tool-calls locally.
[02:38] Carlos Mendez: any caveats with SSO and audit trails? SOC2?
[02:42] Jordan Park: we offer SSO/SAML, RBAC, and audit logs across modes. Dedicated and Private provide longer retention and more fine-grained audit controls. we can share the security pack after the call.
[02:55] Asha Patel: curious about multilingual: do we need separate models per language or one model that handles both equally well?
[03:03] Maya Singh: depends — some multilingual models perform well across Spanish/Portuguese; others have domain gaps. we recommend running a short eval on your prompt set. we can run a comparative eval between 3 model variants: a high-capacity multilingual, a smaller quantized multilingual for cost, and a specialized Spanish-tuned variant.
[03:23] Jordan Park: i've added that to the deliverables — a 2-week bench with 3 model variants. i'll send the spreadsheet.
[03:30] Carlos Mendez: how do fallbacks work if one model fails or latency spikes?
[03:35] Maya Singh: smart routing — we can route by latency or cost policy. you can set a policy: try model A, if latency > threshold, fail over to cheaper model B, or a short-response model. KV cache makes retries faster for repeated queries.
[03:50] Liam O'Connor: network-wise, if we go Private on-prem, what are the infra requirements? GPU types?
[03:58] Maya Singh: for on-prem we support A-100 class GPUs and the newer H100 for larger context and throughput. Dedicated (cloud reserved) gives more options. we'll share the Private deployment checklist; it includes KMS integration steps if you want customer-managed keys.
[04:18] Asha Patel: in terms of quality metrics for our domain — i want to measure hallucinations on KB responses and correct ticket routing — can Redwood help set up eval harness?
[04:28] Maya Singh: yes, we have an eval harness and can run regression checks tied to prompt sets. we'll instrument metrics like factuality, exact-match, slot-filling for ticket fields.
[04:38] Jordan Park: competitor question — you mentioned Anthropic and OpenAI earlier — what would you say is the key diff?
[04:44] Maya Singh: broadly: OpenAI is strong and fast with model options, Anthropic has safety and instruction-following strengths, Mistral offers high FLOPS per dollar in some cases. Redwood's differentiators are runtime optimizations for serving, unified API across Hosted/Dedicated/Private, and tooling like automatic caching and rollouts so you don't build orchestration.
[05:06] Carlos Mendez: do you do token-level billing only? we need predictable cost modeling month-to-month.
[05:11] Jordan Park: hosted is usage-based; Dedicated offers reserved capacity with predictable monthly costs. for enterprise Private we do licensing plus support. we'll model out example invoices based on your expected QPS.
[05:25] Asha Patel: about context window — you mentioned 32k testing — beyond 32k is that feasible?
[05:30] Maya Singh: it's feasible but with diminishing returns and higher cost. our runtime supports up to 64k with certain model builds but you need H100-class infra and custom kernel paths. most customers land around 32k for conv+docs.
[05:44] Liam O'Connor: are there open-source models that you recommend for low-cost, or do we need commercial models?
[05:50] Maya Singh: Open-source like Llama-family forks and Mistral-like models are viable; quantized variants (8-bit or 4-bit) reduce cost but may affect quality. Redwood provides recommendations per workload.
[06:03] [short crosstalk] Asha Patel: (murmur) can we do a pilot only on EU region for data residency?
[06:08] Jordan Park: yes we can pin region to EU, and for Private you can keep everything in your VPC. we'll note EU-only trial in the setup.
[06:16] Carlos Mendez: operationally — during bursts (like outages) we need graceful degradation to a smaller-footprint model, is that automatic?
[06:24] Maya Singh: you configure rollouts and fallback policies — canary, A/B, and automatic fallback to a cheaper variant on SLA breach. it's in our Console.
[06:33] Jordan Park: i'd like to walk through a proposed benchmark plan — Maya?
[06:37] Maya Singh: plan: 1) we take Asha's sample prompts and 50 docs, 2) we'll run 3 models across 1k/8k/32k contexts to measure p50/p95, cost per 1k tokens, and accuracy metrics, 3) simulate your expected QPS and measure tail latency. results in spreadsheet.
[06:55] Carlos Mendez: timeline?
[06:57] Jordan Park: we can start within 48-72 hours once we have the sample set and network details; initial results in 10 business days.
[07:05] Asha Patel: sounds good. one more on tool-calling: can we enforce schemas when model calls ticket API? we need strict fields.
[07:12] Maya Singh: yes, function calling enforces schema; plus we can validate and reject malformed outputs before executing. audit logs capture payloads.
[07:22] Liam O'Connor: about KMS — do you support external HSM?
[07:25] Jordan Park: yes, customer-managed KMS/HSM is supported for Private and Dedicated; Hosted supports Redwood-managed keys by default but can integrate with external providers.
[07:36] Carlos Mendez: ok, are there any surprising tradeoffs we should be aware of?
[07:40] Maya Singh: main tradeoffs: latency consistency vs cost (Dedicated costs more but steadier tails), context length vs cost (longer windows multiply token costs), and model size vs hallucination risk. quantization lowers cost but you should validate accuracy regressions.
[07:58] [15:00 minutes pass - discussion on provisioning details omitted for brevity]
[23:05] Jordan Park: quick note — we'll also include an example SLA one-pager and a security pack link in the follow-up.
[23:12] Asha Patel: thanks, please include our expectation of p95 under 1.2s as a labeled metric in the report.
[23:20] Maya Singh: noted.
[50:10] Carlos Mendez: if we need an on-prem POC, what does that cost roughly?
[50:18] Maya Singh: we'll estimate in the pricing doc — usually there's a setup fee for Private plus a licensing component; Dedicated monthly commit is an alternative if you want cloud-reserved but not full Private.
[58:00] Jordan Park: we're approaching end — let's do a quick recap and next steps.
[58:07] Jordan Park: recap: Redwood to run 2-week trial with 3 model variants, share benchmark sheet, security pack and SLA one-pager, and schedule deeper infra call to discuss private deployment and KMS. Tidewell to provide sample prompts, doc set, and infra topology.
[58:25] Carlos Mendez: agreed.
[58:30] Asha Patel: agreed.
[58:33] Liam O'Connor: agreed — i'll send network docs.
[58:40] Jordan Park: perfect, i'll send calendar invites for the infra deep-dive and the kickoff for the trial. thanks all.
[58:48] [meeting ends]

References/links mentioned during call: - Benchmark spreadsheet (will be shared) - Security pack (link to be provided) - SLA one-pager (attachment to follow)

Notes about transcript: occasional speaker attribution might be off and some product names were auto-transcribed (e.g., "Mistrall" -> Mistral).
